title: Shape a theorem for RH and simple Z

parts:
Please read /papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/notes/09_CONTINUATION_BOOK_PROOF_AND_ARITHMETIC_RELATIVE_FLUX_20261023.md, and the related manuscript book.tex.

We are doing research to improve the results within book.tex, we are not currently working on that manuscript, but we can work on the related main.tex or any other manuscript in the manuscript folder.

The thing that is still missing for me is a theorem that gives a really useful statement about either RH-> simple zeros or RH itself. We don't have to prove either of these statements, but we have to make some progress, and that progress needs to be visible. Otherwise probably no one will want to read the paper. 

So let's try to think about exactly what the theorem should look like. From what I can tell the strongest results are in the RH->simple zeros lane, but correct me if I'm wrong.
I’ll read the continuation note and manuscript, then assess which theorem would give the paper a visible advance. I’ll also get an independent assessment of the RH-to-simplicity lane.

The manuscript has a sharp way to turn a small collision budget into a simplicity bound, but it does not yet prove that the budget is small for zeta. I’m checking what quantitative target would count as a new result, including the existing RH-conditional simplicity bounds.

Your instinct looks right: RH-to-simplicity is the better-supported direction here, especially a statement about the proportion of simple zeros. One distinction matters: `book.tex` measures nonreal zeros before time zero, while `main.tex` has a bounded statistic of real zeros after time zero. Both could support the same headline theorem; neither yet has the arithmetic estimate needed to deliver it.

There is a useful improvement to the theorem target. The book’s bound loses most on triple zeros, while a published RH-conditional multiplicity estimate penalizes triples strongly. Combining them lowers the resource bound needed to beat the known simplicity proportion. I’ve checked the algebra independently and will save this calibration in a research note, leaving the manuscripts unchanged.
We're looking for the best result possible, and are happy to rewrite book.tex if something is superior

Understood. I’ll treat `book.tex` as replaceable and aim for the strongest result the analysis can support. The percentage thresholds are useful diagnostics, not a ceiling. The main target should be RH implying almost-all simplicity, ideally with a quantitative bound on the exceptions; I’m also checking what extra estimate would be needed to reach every-zero simplicity.

Agreed. **The desired theorem should determine the paper, and `book.tex` should be rewritten if a stronger argument emerges.**

Your assessment is broadly right: **RH-to-simplicity is the better-supported direction in the present work.** RH supplies the real-zero geometry needed by the positive-time approach in `main.tex`. The moving-boundary approach in `book.tex` can also address zeros off the critical line, but we have less arithmetic control for that application.

The qualification is that neither manuscript currently proves a new simplicity proportion. They establish ways to convert an arithmetic estimate into one.

**I would aim primarily at quantitative almost-all simplicity under RH.** Write \(N(T)\) for zeros counted with multiplicity and \(N_s(T)\) for simple zeros. The desired statement is

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{RH}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
N(T)-N_s(T)=o(N(T)).}
\]

Ideally, we would prove a rate such as

\[
N(T)-N_s(T)\ll \frac{N(T)}{(\log T)^\delta}
\qquad\text{for some }\delta>0.
\]

The exponent should come from the argument. Even the version without a rate would be a major advance over the established RH-conditional bound \(N_s/N\ge19/27\approx70.37\%\). [Bui–Heath-Brown](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.5018)

This would leave possible sparse multiple zeros. Every-zero simplicity needs an estimate strong enough to exclude one exceptional collision, which the present average estimates do not provide.

There is, however, **a useful strengthening we can make now**, and it changes how demanding the next arithmetic theorem needs to be.

Let \(R(T)\) be the book’s complete cumulative resource: earlier nonreal population plus inward flux, with full endpoint coverage. Let

\[
M(T)=N(T)-N_s(T),\qquad
C(T)=\sum_{\rho\ \mathrm{distinct}}m_\rho(m_\rho-1).
\]

The book gives \(M\le 3R/2\). But we can improve this by combining it with existing arithmetic information:

\[
\boxed{
M(T)\le
\min\left\{C(T),\frac32R(T),\frac{3R(T)+C(T)}4\right\}.
}
\]

The new mixed inequality follows from the elementary bound

\[
m\le \frac34\,2\lfloor m/2\rfloor+\frac14m(m-1),
\qquad m\ge2.
\]

It is exact for both doubles and triples. That matters: **the book’s worst case is a triple, whereas the multiplicity-moment bound’s worst case is a double.** Combining the estimates avoids paying both worst cases separately.

Under RH, Chirre–Gonçalves–de Laat prove

\[
C(T)\le(0.3208+o(1))N(T).
\]

Their notation counts multiplicity differently, but the conversion above is exact. [Theorem 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1810.08843v2)

Consequently, a proved bound \(R(T)\le(r+o(1))N(T)\) gives

\[
\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_s(T)}{N(T)}
\ge
\max\left\{1-\frac32r,\;0.9198-\frac34r\right\}.
\]

This gives useful checkpoints:

| Arithmetic resource bound | Simplicity consequence under RH |
|---|---:|
| \(r<0.288128395\ldots\) | Improves \(19/27\) |
| \(r=1/4\) | At least \(73.23\%\) simple |
| \(r=0.2264\) | At least \(75\%\) simple |
| \(r\to0\) | Almost every zero simple |

These percentages are **milestones, not the objective’s ceiling**. The improvement here is a stronger conversion theorem; we have not yet proved any of those resource bounds for theta.

For the strongest objective, I think the substantive theorem to attack should look like this:

> **Proposed microscopic stability theorem.** Assume RH. At explicitly prescribed backward times proportional to \(-\lambda/(\log h)^2\) on height-\(h\) bands, construct complete windows whose total resource satisfies
> \[
> \limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{R_T(\lambda)}{N(T)}
> \le A(\lambda),
> \qquad A(\lambda)\longrightarrow0
> \quad(\lambda\downarrow0).
> \]

This would imply almost-all simplicity. An explicit modulus and a sufficiently uniform height error could yield a quantitative exceptional-count bound.

The order of limits is essential: first increasing height at a fixed prescribed microscopic scale, then shrinking that scale. Choosing the time after examining the unknown multiple zeros would merely repackage the conclusion. The theorem must **prove the resource estimate from RH and actual theta/xi arithmetic**, including the earlier population, flux and coverage costs.

I would keep both existing approaches available while pursuing that estimate:

- **The book’s resource** has a clear collision interpretation and now benefits from the mixed multiplicity bound above.
- **The positive-time statistic in `main.tex`** has more concrete microscopic Riemann–Siegel infrastructure and uses RH to retain real-root positivity. Its missing arithmetic estimate is still substantial.

There is not yet enough evidence to declare either approach superior. The deciding result should be an arithmetic bound with useful size—not the elegance of its representation.

**My recommendation is to make almost-all simplicity under RH the principal theorem target, pursue the strongest quantitative exception bound available, and let the successful estimate reorganize the manuscript.** The mixed bound gives us a better intermediate route without lowering that ambition.

I saved the derivation, precise targets and control checks in [Research Note 10](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-4/12_height_dependent_heat_contours/brainstorm/notes/10_SIMPLICITY_THEOREM_TARGETS_AND_HYBRID_CONSUMER_20261023.md).

Make sure that the flexibility in the theorem is apparent in the research overview. We are not necessarily looking for a well-characterized theorem, we are looking for the best result we can find to support RH->simple zeros

I’ll write the overview around the strongest analytic result we can find toward RH implying simple zeros, keeping the theorem’s form open. I’ll pair it with a progress register that separates established results, open estimates, and supporting work.

I’m making the theorem’s flexibility explicit: density-one simplicity, a stronger proportion, eventual simplicity, or a useful local restriction are possible outcomes, not a required sequence. The register will track three overarching goals—prove a useful arithmetic estimate, derive its strongest simplicity consequence, and build the paper around that proof. The existing flux and spectral programs will remain available as supporting approaches.

The drafts now leave room for the analytic exploration to change both the theorem and the method. A separate review caught two points I’m tightening: the percentage comparisons need an explicit asymptotic bound, and routine proof exploration should not require a formal task declaration. I’m also adding links so future sessions find this broader program without restarting completed flux work.
